# Prescriptive lessons -- randy-felts x reharmonization-techniques

## maj7

Felts treats the major-seventh chord as the tonal home base of all jazz harmony: IMaj7 anchors the tonic family, is the mandatory destination of extended endings, and sets the notational floor (seventh chords replace triads everywhere). His maj7 rules are largely about protecting that stability--restricting line cliches to the tonic, demanding root-position context before third inversions, and prescribing simplified symbols when slash-chord notation obscures function.

- [ch.1 p.6 / ch.8 p.74] IMaj7 anchors the tonic family alongside III-7 and VI-7; all three are stable (no scale-degree 4) and interchangeable for simple substitution or as the opening slot of a turnaround.
- [ch.7 p.65-66] Seventh chords replace bare triads as the notational baseline; writing IMaj7 and IVMaj7 instead of I and IV makes harmonic function legible to performers.
- [ch.1 p.6 / ch.9 p.87] III-7 and VI-7 carry full tonic function and substitute for IMaj7 in simple substitution, turnarounds, extended endings, and modulatory interludes.
- [ch.9 p.86] Extended endings must resolve to a final Maj7 chord in a new key via deceptive cadence; the target quality is specifically Maj7--not dominant or minor.
- [ch.1 p.11] IVMaj7 tolerates a #4/tritone in the melody while II-7 does not; melody compatibility overrides family-membership substitution permission.
- [ch.7 p.67] Diatonic tensions 9 and 13 are stylistically implied on Maj7 chords and should be omitted from the symbol; writing them explicitly implies a prescribed voicing.
- [ch.11 p.109] Line cliches (chromatic half-step motion through the fifth and root) are normatively applied to the tonic I chord; using them elsewhere risks making the embellished chord sound like a new tonic.
- [ch.7 p.70] Overly complex slash symbols like E-7/C obscure tonic function; simplify to CMaj7 when it more clearly reveals the vertical harmony.
- [ch.2 p.22] bVIIMaj7 is the one non-diatonic chord permitted in diatonic approach technique, borrowed from the parallel Dorian scale; it blends smoothly without overpowering other diatonic choices.
- [ch.13 p.123-145] In Lydian modal reharmonization, the characteristic #11 requires a tonic pedal; without it the listener reads the dissonance as a structural error rather than a modal color.
- [ch.6 p.55 / ch.10 p.101] Third-inversion Maj7 (seventh in the bass) requires an immediately preceding root-position form; absent that context, the ear builds a new chord on the bass note.

---

## min7

Felts treats minor-seventh chords as functionally ambiguous--they carry tonic function (III-7, VI-7) or subdominant function (II-7) depending on position, but both contexts are tightly gated by the b9 and tritone proscriptions. The dominant chain and displacement sections show min7 as a textural softener and a melodic recontextualization engine; the modal and bass-line sections impose hard upper limits on how many can appear consecutively without destroying key sense.

- [ch.1 p.6-7] III-7 and VI-7 belong to the tonic family; II-7 belongs to the subdominant family. All three are valid simple substitutions for their family members, subject to b9 and tritone gate conditions.
- [ch.1 p.11] (Proscriptive) Avoid 13 or b13 in the lead of II-7; the 13 creates a tritone with the chord's third, and reserving that energy for the following V7 produces a more satisfying cadential flow.
- [ch.1 p.11] (Proscriptive) The tritone (#4/b11) melody/harmony interval is disallowed on any minor-seventh chord; it destroys subdominant or tonic function by making the chord sound dominant.
- [ch.3 p.31-33] The most common interpolated chord in an extended dominant chain is a minor seventh placed between two dominants; it briefly delays resolution and smooths texture compared to an unbroken dominant chain.
- [ch.4 p.40-41] When a min7 with b3 in the melody lead is displaced upward by a half-step II-V7 pattern, the b3 is recontextualized as tension 9 on the inserted II-7.
- [ch.4 p.40-41] When a min7 with b5 in the melody lead is displaced upward by a half-step II-V7, the b5 becomes tension 11 on the inserted II-7.
- [ch.6 p.54] Bass notes implying min7 chords must be treated as chord tones (1, 3, 5, 7), not extensions; extension bass notes produce hybrid voicings or unwieldy symbols.
- [ch.12 p.119] A chromatic II-V7 pattern pairs a min7 (or min7b5) with a dominant seventh a half step below; root motion is chromatic and the pair functions as subdominant-to-dominant.
- [ch.5 p.45-52] (Proscriptive) Minor-quality modal interchange chords clash with melodies containing the major third, producing a b9 interval; melody compatibility governs all MI substitutions.
- [ch.5 p.45-52] (Proscriptive) Use no more than three consecutive modal interchange chords before returning to diatonic harmony; exceeding this limit erodes the listener's sense of home key.
- [ch.13 p.124] In Dorian modal reharmonization, I-7 occupies strong rhythmic positions approached by the mode-specific II-7 -> I-7 cadence; the modal key must persist for at least four bars.
- [ch.11 p.109] (Proscriptive) Repeated line cliches on a non-tonic minor seventh chord risk causing the listener to hear it as a new I chord, weakening key sense.

---

## min7b5

Felts positions min7b5 primarily as a dominant-family surrogate (VII-7b5) and as the subdominant slot of the chromatic II-V7 pattern, while flatly forbidding it as an upper-layer hybrid structure. Its two displacement rules mirror those of min7, differing only in that b5 is the specific melody note triggering the tension-11 transformation.

- [ch.1 p.7] VII-7(b5) belongs to the dominant family alongside V7--both share the tritone formed by scale degrees 4 and 7--and may substitute for V7 in dominant-family contexts.
- [ch.4 p.41] When b5 appears in the lead of a min7(b5) chord and the chord is displaced by a half-step II-V7, the b5 converts to tension 11 on the II-7 of the inserted pattern.
- [ch.12 p.119] A min7(b5) may serve as the II chord in a chromatic II-V7 pattern, paired with a dominant seventh a half step below.
- [ch.14 p.147] (Proscriptive) Do not use a min7(b5) structure as the upper layer of a hybrid voicing; combined with the bass note it collapses into a recognizable traditional voicing rather than the intended ambiguous altered-dominant texture.

---

## dom7

Dominant sevenths are the engine of the book's cadential and reharmonization machinery. Felts codes them as tritone-driven resolution forces, freely substitutable by their tritone-partner subV7, and the mandatory final slot of every turnaround. Every technique that adds harmonic motion--displacement, extended chains, diminished reharmonization--runs through the dominant seventh as its terminal or medial chord.

- [ch.1 p.7] V7 is the primary dominant-family chord; its forward motion derives from the tritone between scale degrees 4 and 7, and it almost always precedes phrase endings.
- [ch.3 p.28] Any dominant seventh may be replaced by the dominant seventh a tritone away (subV7); both share the same tritone.
- [ch.4 p.37] Cadential dominant sevenths are the preferred targets for displacement; moving them later in the phrase creates a noticeable shift in harmonic shape.
- [ch.4 p.37] Displaced dominant sevenths may be approached by: a related II-7 (forming II-V7), another dominant a perfect fifth above, a dominant a half step higher, or any other technique in the book.
- [ch.3 p.30-32] (Proscriptive) At medium-to-fast tempos, chords in extended dominant chains should appear only on strong beats (1 and 3); placing them on every beat creates hyperactive harmonic rhythm.
- [ch.3 p.29-30] Altered tensions (b9, #9, b5, b13) on dominants resolve most often downward; upward motion requires contextual justification.
- [ch.3 p.35] Extended dominant and II-V7 techniques work best when the melody consists mainly of quarter, dotted quarter, or half notes; sparse melody notes allow clashes to resolve quickly.
- [ch.8 p.74] The fourth and final slot of every turnaround template must carry dominant function resolving by strong root motion into the next phrase; this is non-negotiable.
- [ch.12 p.113-119] Four dominant sevenths are related to any given diminished seventh; selection follows a three-tier hierarchy: shared tritone -> strong cadential root motion to the target -> maximum shared chord tones.
- [ch.10 p.96] When root motion moves by perfect fourth or fifth, resolve chord tone 3 of the dominant to chord tone 7 of the next chord, and chord tone 7 to chord tone 3.
- [ch.1 p.10 / ch.2 p.23] (Proscriptive) Any substitution creating a b9 interval between melody and a chord tone of a dominant seventh is disallowed; only V7(b9) resolving to I is exempt.
- [ch.3 p.33] In extended dominant chains, dominants falling on strong beats may be converted to minor sevenths to smooth texture, generating extended II-V7 patterns from extended dominant patterns.
- [ch.6 p.55-56] Third-inversion dominant seventh (seventh in the bass) requires an immediately preceding root-position form; absent that context the chord is heard as built on the bass note.

---

## dom7b9

Felts carves out a single narrow exemption to the universal b9 prohibition: V7(b9) resolving to I is accepted precisely because the b9 pairs with the tritone and both tones follow established downward resolution paths into the tonic.

- [ch.1 p.10] V7(b9) is the only common exception to the universal rule against b9 melody/harmony intervals; the b9 is licensed because it combines with the tritone and both resolve predictably into IMaj7.

---

## dom7alt

Felts treats the altered dominant sound as a hybrid-voicing product derived from the altered dominant scale, deployable only at phrase endpoints and invalidated the moment the melody reveals a major or minor third above the bass.

- [ch.14 p.147] Hybrid chord voicings produce an altered dominant texture derived from the altered dominant scale (1, b9, #9, 3, #4/b5, b6, b7); the mechanism is a triad or seventh chord layered above a fixed bass root.
- [ch.14 p.149] (Proscriptive) Hybrid altered-dominant voicings lose their effectiveness when the melody contains a major or minor third above the bass note; that interval collapses the ambiguous texture.
- [ch.14 p.149] Hybrid altered-dominant voicings work most effectively at phrase endpoints rather than throughout a passage; they function as deliberate tonal tools deployed for contrast.

---

## dom7sus4

Felts assigns sus4 a rare dual family membership and uses it as both a notational clarification tool and a displacement repair mechanism when a fourth appears in the melody.

- [ch.1 p.7] V7sus4 belongs to both the subdominant family (the suspended fourth eliminates the tritone) and the dominant family (when it resolves directly to IMaj7); context determines function.
- [ch.4 p.39] When displacement creates a melody/harmony clash because the melody contains a fourth, adjust the chord quality to sus4 to accommodate it.
- [ch.7 p.70] Slash symbols like D-7/G may be rewritten as G7sus4 when the latter more clearly reveals harmonic function.

---

## dim7

Felts treats diminished seventh chords primarily as disguised dominant sevenths awaiting reharmonization; all three reharmonization rules systematically reduce ambiguity by locating the implied dominant. He also uses dim7 as a notational diagnostic: a chain of diminished sevenths may be hiding a line cliche.

- [ch.12 p.113-115] Diminished sevenths are reharmonized by replacing them with one of four related dominant sevenths, each sharing one of the diminished seventh's two tritones.
- [ch.12 p.116-117] Diminished sevenths that move up by half step to a root-position chord are most often reharmonized with a dominant a perfect fifth or minor second above the target.
- [ch.12 p.117-119] When no obvious dominant cadence connects the related dominant to the target, choose the dominant sharing the greatest number of chord tones with the original diminished seventh.
- [ch.7 p.68-69] Any diminished seventh can be spelled as four enharmonically equal symbols; harmonic context and function determine the correct spelling.
- [ch.7 p.69] Two signals indicate a hidden line cliche inside a diminished-seventh chain: (1) a secondary dominant with augmented quality, and (2) a diminished seventh that does not resolve by step.
- [ch.14 p.147] (Proscriptive) Do not use a diminished structure as the upper layer of a hybrid voicing; it collapses into a recognizable traditional voicing rather than the intended ambiguous altered-dominant texture.

---

## aug

Felts mentions augmented structures solely in the context of what not to do inside hybrid voicings; no prescriptive use is documented elsewhere in the text.

- [ch.14 p.147] (Proscriptive) Do not use an augmented triad as the upper layer of a hybrid voicing; augmented upper-layer structures combine with the bass note to produce sounds resembling traditional chord voicings rather than the intended ambiguous texture.

---

## min-maj7

Felts introduces min-maj7 solely as one of twelve modal interchange colors available in a major-key context, drawn from the parallel harmonic minor scale, without elaborating specific voice-leading constraints beyond the general MI melody-compatibility rule.

- [ch.5 p.45-52] I-(Maj7) is one of twelve common modal interchange chords available in a major key, drawn from parallel harmonic minor; it introduces color via new chord tones while remaining subject to the b9 melody-compatibility constraint.

---

## triad

Felts treats bare triads as a notational failure mode with no place in jazz harmonic vocabulary.

- [ch.7 p.65] (Proscriptive) Bare triadic chord symbols are stylistically incorrect for jazz standards; seventh chords are the minimum acceptable notational baseline.
